power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background.
African, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities in Canada experience a disproportionate burden of HIV, and a considerable share of infections among ACB immigrants is acquired after arrival in Canada.
Yet how ACB people themselves understand the structural circumstances surrounding post-migration acquisition remains underexamined.
This study asked how intersecting structural and social disadvantages shape post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities in Ontario.
We conducted an interpretive secondary thematic analysis of 44 in-depth interviews from the MSAFIRI Study, read through intersectionality and structural-vulnerability lenses.
Interviews were coded inductively and deductively by two analysts, with consensus adjudication and community review of the thematic structure.
Results.

Five structural conditions organized participants' accounts: racism as a structural condition of settlement; immigration precarity and the work of settling alone; economic precarity, including insecure work, poverty, and unstable housing; ruptured kin networks and isolation under migration; and gendered violence and homophobia.
These conditions compounded one another, so that disadvantage in one domain deepened vulnerability in another.
Post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities is produced by intersecting structural disadvantages encountered in the receiving country context.

Equitable HIV prevention requires structural and community-led responses that address immigration precarity, economic and housing insecurity, gendered violence, homophobia, and anti-Black racism, alongside biomedical and individual-level prevention.
African, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities continue to experience a disproportionate burden of HIV in Canada, and particularly in Ontario (Mbuagbaw et al., 2026).
text.formatted: African, Caribbean, and Black (ACB) communities continue to experience a disproportionate burden of HIV in Canada, and particularly in Ontario <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Mbuagbaw et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although ACB populations represent a relatively small share of the Canadian population, they account for a markedly higher proportion of HIV diagnoses (Statistics Canada, 2024; Public Health Agency of Canada, 2026).
text.formatted: Although ACB populations represent a relatively small share of the Canadian population, they account for a markedly higher proportion of HIV diagnoses <ref type="bibr">(Statistics Canada, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Public Health Agency of Canada, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This disparity reflects longstanding inequities rooted in racism, economic marginalization, and exclusionary social policies, not any inherent feature of ACB communities (Odhiambo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This disparity reflects longstanding inequities rooted in racism, economic marginalization, and exclusionary social policies, not any inherent feature of ACB communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Odhiambo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A considerable share of these infections is acquired after migration.

In Ontario, an estimated 20% to 30% of immigrants from sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean who are living with HIV are thought to have acquired HIV after arriving in Canada (Ontario HIV Treatment Network [OHTN], 2016), and the MSAFIRI Study has documented the relational and sexual circumstances of post-arrival acquisition among ACB immigrants (Tharao et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In Ontario, an estimated 20% to 30% of immigrants from sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean who are living with HIV are thought to have acquired HIV after arriving in Canada <ref type="bibr">(Ontario HIV Treatment Network [OHTN], 2016)</ref>, and the MSAFIRI Study has documented the relational and sexual circumstances of post-arrival acquisition among ACB immigrants <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Tharao et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This evidence challenges the assumption that HIV among ACB people is primarily imported from countries of origin and redirects attention toward the conditions ACB migrants encounter following settlement.
Understanding those conditions is therefore central to any equitable HIV prevention response.
This reorientation toward the receiving country context is consistent with a growing international literature.

European estimates of post-migration acquisition among African and Caribbean migrants range from 2% to 63%, depending on the population and the method of estimation (Fakoya et al., 2015; Alvarez-del Arco et al., 2017; Gosselin et al., 2020), and postmigration acquisition has been linked to immigration precarity, housing instability, economic marginalization, and obstacles to healthcare access.

text.text: North American evidence similarly implicates institutional and social contexts.

Gendered patterns of service provision, including the limited representation and engagement of heterosexual ACB men within HIV prevention and support services, restrict access to HIV-related information, resources, and care (Baidoobonso et al., 2013).

text.text: Vulnerability is thus shaped not only by individual circumstances but by the ways institutions and services are organized and made accessible to different groups within ACB communities.
Recognizing this, scholars have increasingly called for a departure from the behavioral frameworks that have long dominated HIV research and prevention.

Such frameworks locate risk within individual knowledge, attitudes, and practices (J. K. Williams et al., 2009) and have too often encouraged deficit-oriented narratives that portray racialized communities as inherently vulnerable because of their behaviors, cultures, or beliefs.

Williams and colleagues (2009) argue that effective HIV prevention for Black women in Canada requires moving beyond risk-reduction models focused on individual behavior toward approaches that address the forces patterning health inequities.

text.text: A structural perspective thus shifts attention from what individuals do to the conditions under which choices become possible, constrained, or consequential.

text.text: Together, these frameworks locate HIV vulnerability within broader structures of power rather than within individual behavior alone.
Despite a growing body of literature on HIV among ACB communities in Canada, much of this scholarship has concentrated on HIV testing, prevention, risk behaviors, and individuallevel interventions.
Little is known about how ACB people themselves understand the structural circumstances surrounding HIV acquisition after migration.
This study examined how intersecting structural and social disadvantages shaped post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB people living with HIV in Ontario.

The specific objectives were to: (1) describe the structural and social conditions that participants identified as surrounding their HIV acquisition after migration; (2) examine how these conditions intersected to shape vulnerability; and (3) identify implications for HIV prevention, practice, and policy.
We drew on a secondary qualitative analysis of 44 interviews from the MSAFIRI Study and interpreted participants' accounts through intersectional and structural-vulnerability lenses.

This is a qualitative secondary analysis of the MSAFIRI Study, informed by the intersectional and structural-vulnerability frameworks outlined above (Crenshaw, 1989 (Crenshaw, , 1991;; Farmer et al., 2006; Quesada et al., 2011).

text.text: Analytically, this meant treating racism, immigration policy, labor-market precarity, housing, and gendered power as the conditions under which ACB people came to be at risk, and reading these axes as co-constitutive rather than additive.

MSAFIRI was a mixed-methods study of post-migration HIV acquisition among ACB communities in Ontario, comprising a cross-sectional survey (n = 108) and in-depth, semistructured interviews with a subsample of 44 survey participants.
Participants were recruited through purposive sampling from the Ontario HIV Treatment Network Cohort Study (OCS) across five HIV clinics in Toronto and Ottawa between January 2015 and March 2017.
Interviews explored migration and settlement, relationships, health decision-making, and the circumstances surrounding HIV acquisition.

text.text: In participants' narratives, anti-Black racism was not an isolated incident but a pervasive condition that shaped their lives from childhood or from arrival in Canada onward, influencing where they felt they belonged and how much effort daily life required of them.
Several participants described racism encountered on arrival as something they had to absorb and adapt around.
One woman who migrated from the Caribbean to Québec recalled: "I was called 'Chocolate'… I was teased a lot, especially in Québec.
Black people had it really hard… I grew a thick skin to be able to stay" (woman, Caribbean).
Her account locates the harm in the receiving environment, in schools and among peers, and describes the "thick skin" she had to develop in order to stay.

A Canadian-born participant of mixed ACB heritage described racism reaching back to early childhood: "I dealt with a lot of racial tension… people were very, very prejudice when I was growing up… I remember asking my grandmother what colour my blood was" (woman, Canadian-born).
Her question to her grandmother shows how early she came to see her difference as a question of worth.
This experience of racism began long before any sexual encounter and shaped the sense of self she brought to later health decisions.
Together, these accounts position racism as a foundational condition that shaped settlement, belonging, and self-concept, and that operated through institutions and communities.
Immigration status operated as a master condition that governed security, mobility, and access to basic supports, often leaving people to navigate unfamiliar systems without a map.
Participants described status itself as a source of chronic uncertainty.
One woman recalled: "your immigration status, that's if they accept you or no, you don't know.
You don't know to be settled really here or no.
You don't know what is going on in your life" (woman, sub-Saharan Africa).
Her words render precarity as an ongoing state of suspension in which planning, including for health, is foreclosed by a decision held elsewhere.
Others described settling with no institutional scaffolding at all.
A man who arrived through Montréal recounted: "I didn't even know there was something like shelter.
They didn't tell me… somebody told me I have to go to welfare.
I don't know about welfare… So you had to figure everything out on your own" (man, sub-Saharan Africa).

The system into which he arrived furnished neither information nor support, so survival depended on chance encounters with strangers, conditions that crowd out preventive health engagement; he later noted that he saw a doctor "only when I'm sick."
Across these accounts, immigration precarity produced vulnerability by removing stability and withholding the information needed to reach the resources that make protective choices possible.
Insecure work and the poverty and housing instability that followed it repeatedly narrowed participants' room to maneuver during the period surrounding acquisition.
Job loss could cascade quickly into deeper precarity.
One woman recounted: "I found out that I was pregnant… so then I became jobless… I moved to her house and then from her house I went to live in a shelter" (woman, sub-Saharan Africa).
The sequence of pregnancy, job loss, dependence, and shelter shows how quickly economic insecurity stripped away options and how little buffer existed between employment and homelessness.
A second participant described the churn of insecure work: "I had been fired from probably the best job I ever had… I was going from job to job.
At this point, I had no job" (man, Canadian-born).
His account conveys how the loss of stable employment unsettled the wider life context within which health and relationships were managed.
These narratives show economic precarity constraining housing, stability, and bargaining power, so that what is conventionally termed "risk" was lived inside material constraints.
Migration frequently severed participants from the kin networks that elsewhere would have buffered hardship, leaving people to face settlement, illness, and risk with thinned support.
The geographic scattering of family was a recurring structural feature.
One woman stated plainly: "Back home, it's where my whole family is.
In Canada, I have none" (woman, sub-Saharan Africa).

Her account locates isolation in the structure of migration itself: her family was absent by border, and that absence removed a first line of practical and emotional support at the very time settlement was hardest.

For others, isolation compounded with the demands of survival work: "I lost contact with my sister, which is the one I was closest to… we were workaholics… most times I get up, go to work, by the time I come home it's very late… It's like a machine" (man, Caribbean).

Here the erosion of close ties is bound up with labour conditions that consumed time and energy, so that the work required to survive in Canada corroded the relationships that might have sustained him.

Across these accounts, ruptured kin networks emerge as a structurally produced exposure: migration and precarious work hollowed out the support systems through which people would otherwise have weathered risk.

Gendered power and heteronormativity operated as structural forces in participants' accounts, surfacing as IPV and sexual coercion in women's narratives and as homophobia and its transnational criminalization in the narratives of sexual-minority men.
Both constrained the capacity to refuse, disclose, know, or seek help.
For several women, exposure occurred through a 13 partner's coercion and concealment.
One woman described a husband who knew his status and refused both protection and treatment: "I asked him for several times to use a condom… he was asking by his doctor to take the medication.
He didn't take… That's why I say he did it by purpose" (woman, sub-Saharan Africa).

Her account renders acquisition as the outcome of coercive control within marriage: she sought protection repeatedly and was overridden by a partner whose non-disclosure operated through a gendered imbalance of power.
For sexual-minority men, vulnerability was frequently structured by homophobia that long predated any encounter and reached across borders.

One bisexual man described the conditions that pushed his sexuality and sexual health into silence: "being Jamaican and saying that you're into guys… was a huge problem so I just never [brought it up]… homosexuality in the south is banned and HIV and homosexuality go hand in hand, so all that stuff is just hushhush and not brought to light" (man, Caribbean).
Here criminalization, communal silence, and the stigmatized coupling of HIV with same-sex desire foreclosed open identity and access to sexual-health knowledge.
These legal, familial, and communal forms of homophobia shaped his risk.

These accounts position gendered violence and homophobia as structural determinants on the same footing as racism, immigration precarity, and poverty: they governed who could negotiate safety and who was silenced into risk.

Where participants voiced self-blame for these exposures, we read such statements as evidence of internalized structural narratives, and the analysis locates responsibility in the violence and the systems that enabled it.
These conditions did not operate in isolation.

They compounded, as when a woman navigating immigration precarity and isolation also negotiated a coercive partner, or a man managing racism and economic insecurity was also silenced by homophobia, so that disadvantage in one domain intensified vulnerability in another.
Participants were not passive before these conditions; they adapted, endured, and at times resisted.
Yet their capacity to protect their health was shaped by the structures that surrounded them.
This study examined how intersecting structural and social disadvantages shape postmigration HIV vulnerability among ACB communities in Ontario.

Across 44 in-depth interviews, participants located the conditions surrounding acquisition in racism, immigration precarity, economic precarity, ruptured kin networks, and gendered violence and homophobia.

Estimates that 20% to 30% of HIV among sub-Saharan African and Caribbean immigrants in Ontario is acquired after arrival (OHTN, 2016), alongside European estimates ranging from 2% to 63% (Fakoya et al., 2015; Gosselin et al., 2020), establish that post-migration acquisition is substantial.

text.text: The central contribution of this analysis is to show that post-migration HIV vulnerability among ACB participants was produced by structural conditions operating together.

This patterning is best understood through intersectionality, which holds that racism, gendered power, heteronormativity, and immigration-related exclusion are co-constitutive (Crenshaw, 1989 (Crenshaw, , 1991;; Bowleg, 2012).

The present analysis examines the period surrounding acquisition and shows that the same structures implicated in post-diagnosis marginalization were already shaping exposure before diagnosis.

Anti-Black racism, in particular, operated as a pervasive condition that shaped settlement, belonging, and self-concept from childhood or from arrival in Canada, which supports calls to treat racism as a fundamental cause of health inequity (K. K. A. Williams et al., 2024).

text.text: By foregrounding conditions encountered after arrival, the findings reframe a persistent narrative that attributes HIV among ACB communities to importation from countries of origin.
Participants' accounts of status insecurity, labour-market exclusion, unstable housing, and severed kin networks describe a receiving country context that generated vulnerability.

This interpretation converges with European evidence linking post-migration acquisition to immigration precarity, economic marginalization, and barriers to care (Fakoya et al., 2015; Alvarez-del Arco et al., 2017; Gosselin et al., 2020), and with Canadian research showing how legislative exclusion and precarious status produce structural barriers to HIV care for ACB immigrants (Gagnon et al., 2022; Odhiambo et al., 2022 Odhiambo et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Our contribution is to demonstrate that these same structural forces shape vulnerability upstream of diagnosis, during the process of settlement itself, and to do so from the standpoint of ACB people.

The limited engagement of heterosexual ACB men with HIV services noted in prior Canadian work (Baidoobonso et al., 2013; Etowa, Etowa, et al., 2022; Nelson et al., 2019) is echoed in accounts of men who encountered systems that furnished neither information nor support, underscoring that access is structured well before any individual decision about testing or protection.

text.text: A consistent analytic commitment of this study was to resist deficit-oriented readings that locate HIV risk in the behaviours, cultures, or beliefs of racialized communities.
Participants grew "a thick skin," pieced together survival without institutional support, and at times named and resisted the injustices they faced.
A structural lens reads such agency as exercised within, and constrained by, arrangements that distributed the capacity to protect one's health unequally.

This orientation is consistent with community priorities and with structural approaches that call for prevention to move beyond individual risk reduction toward the conditions that pattern health inequities (Latkin et al., 2010; C. C. Williams et al., 2009; Bowleg, 2012; Etowa, Tharao, et al., 2022).

text.text: Recognizing both agency and constraint is central to a structural-vulnerability analysis.
If vulnerability is produced structurally, then prevention must be structural as well.

Biomedical tools such as pre-exposure prophylaxis and treatment as prevention remain essential, but their reach depends on the very conditions participants lacked: stable status, secure housing, economic footing, trustworthy services, and freedom from violence.
Several implications follow.

First, immigration status should be treated as a modifiable determinant of HIV vulnerability, with attention to expanding healthcare eligibility and reducing the insecurity generated by precarious status (Gagnon et al., 2022; Odhiambo et al., 2022 Odhiambo et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Second, responses to economic and housing precarity, including access to stable housing and income support during settlement, are HIV-prevention measures insofar as they restore the material ground on which protective choices become possible.

Third, services must address gendered violence and homophobia directly, through trauma-informed and IPV-responsive care for ACB women and through affirming, confidential services for sexual-minority ACB men whose exposure was structured by criminalization and communal silence (Fseifes & Etowa, 2023; Logie et al., 2011).

text.text: This study has several limitations.

As a secondary analysis, it was bounded by data generated for the parent study's purposes; interviews were not designed to elicit every structural domain examined here, and questions tailored to this analytic focus might have yielded further detail.
The interviews were conducted between 2015 and 2017, and aspects of the immigration and service context have since changed, although the structural conditions described remain salient.

As a qualitative study grounded in the accounts of 44 ACB people living with HIV in two Ontario cities, the analysis prioritizes transferability and conceptual insight rather than statistical generalizability.
Finally, the analytic sample includes Canadian-born participants of ACB parentage, retained for the reasons set out in the Methods.

Their experiences of "postmigration" vulnerability differ from those of foreign-born participants, and the sample was not large enough to analyze nativity strata in depth; findings should therefore be read as speaking to ACB diasporic communities broadly rather than to foreign-born migrants alone.
Ontario is the cumulative, intersecting outcome of structural conditions encountered in the receiving context.

Racism, immigration precarity, economic and housing insecurity, ruptured kin networks, and gendered violence and homophobia converged to distribute the capacity to protect one's health unequally, well before acquisition occurred.

Equitable HIV prevention therefore requires structural and community-led responses that address these conditions directly, alongside biomedical tools, and that challenge the deficit narratives participants' lives so clearly refute.
